newsitem.title: USA: Conn. aims to eliminate insurance fund liability.
newsitem.headline: Conn. aims to eliminate insurance fund liability.

text.p: Connecticut's state treasurer said that the state aims to eliminate the long-term liability on its so-called Second Injury Fund, estimated as high as $7 billion in 1994, in the next couple of years.
By settling outstanding cases at around six cents on the dollar, the state already has shrunk the fund's liability by about $1 billion.
And as part of its privatization plan, it has approved borrowing as much as $750 million, which includes a $100 million sale of revenue bonds slated for the end of the month.

Christopher Burnham, the state treasurer, on Monday told a Bond Buyer conference on public finance in New England that he expected to settle the rest of the cases at from five to 10 cents a dollar by early July 1999.
"I believe that liability in the next two years will be at zero," he added, referring to the approximately $5.5 billion liability.
The Second Injury Fund, set up in 1945 to encourage employers to hire veterans and others with pre-existing medical conditions, acted like a workers' compensation fund.

Burnham said that the fund, in addition to Connecticut's unfunded pension liability, which was estimated at as high as $6.5 billion, likely were some of the biggest concerns that rating agencies and underwriters had about the state's finances.

Connecticut has worked hard to restructure its pension fund, which totaled around $10.5 billion when the current state treasurer took office in 1994, and had nearly as many managers as California's $98 billion fund, Burnham said.

The Connecticut official added the fund's performance had improved since he cut the number of managers and staff, while its assets have climbed to $14 billion. His goal is for the fund to reach $20 billion before the end of his term.

The rising stock market has buoyed the pension funds of a number of states, including Connecticut, but Burnham added that the Rowland Administration was trying to get unions for state and municipal employees and teachers to switch to less costly defined contribution plans from the current defined benefit plans.
The move would slash how much Connecticut contributes per employee to $5,000 to $6,000 a year from $7,000 to $11,000, he noted.
However, Connecticut officials sounded a cautionary note when asked about the impact of baby-boomers, whom actuaries expect to live longer lives than their parents. Reuter
